expectedText:
TRUST AMENDMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Alameda County

DECLARATION IDENTIFYING THE ORIGINAL TRUST AND THE AMENDMENT
I, Jordan Alex Lee, of Alameda County County, California, as settlor, declare this instrument to be an amendment to the The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust, dated March 14, 2020 (the "Trust"). I identify below the specific provision(s) of the Trust that this amendment adds, deletes, or amends, and the new text of each: ☐ _________________________. This amendment is effective as of September 1, 2026.

THE SETTLOR'S STATUTORY POWER TO MODIFY A REVOCABLE TRUST
Once The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust exists as a trust revocable by Jordan Alex Lee, California's Probate Code gives Jordan Alex Lee an independent statutory power to modify it, separate from the power to revoke it outright. Unless The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's own instrument provides otherwise, Jordan Alex Lee may modify The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust by following the same procedure the Probate Code provides for revoking it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, if a trust is revocable by the settlor, the settlor may modify the trust by the procedure for revocation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15402 (California Legislative Information text), the settlor's statutory power to modify a revocable trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a settlor's power to modify a revocable trust -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. The statute's current text is a single sentence, and that sentence does not itself offer 'a signed writing delivered to the trustee' as one alternative among several, with an additional catch-all allowing modification by any method that shows clear and convincing evidence of the settlor's intent. That broader 'clear and convincing evidence of intent' standard appears in some other states' trust statutes and in the Restatement (Third) of Trusts, but was not found in the current text of California Probate Code section 15402 itself -- so this document does not attribute that language to section 15402. What the modification power actually incorporates is whatever procedure a separate statute sets out for revocation, quoted in a different clause of this document. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 15402); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE PROCEDURE FOR REVOCATION, INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE FOR MODIFICATION
Because The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's modification power works 'by the procedure for revocation,' the specific procedure that power incorporates comes from a separate Probate Code section governing revocation. That section provides two routes: compliance with whatever revocation method The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's own instrument sets out, or -- if The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one -- a writing, other than a will, signed by Jordan Alex Lee and delivered to Jordan Alex Lee during Jordan Alex Lee's lifetime.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory methods of revocation, incorporated by section 15402 for modification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedure California's modification statute incorporates by reference -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This same statutory section, Probate Code section 15401, is also the source for a separate clause of this document addressing a trust with more than one settlor; that clause quotes a different subdivision -- (b) -- of this same section, rather than an independent source, and this disclosure is made there as well. A further subdivision of this section, (e), also states that a trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987 is governed by prior law rather than by this section; this document does not independently research what that prior law required.

WHEN THE TRUST INSTRUMENT MAKES ITS OWN AMENDMENT METHOD EXCLUSIVE
If The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's own instrument states, in explicit terms, that its stated amendment or revocation method is the exclusive method, then the fallback method -- a signed writing delivered to Jordan Alex Lee -- is not available; only the method the instrument itself specifies will do. A published California Court of Appeal decision, applying this same statutory framework, has summarized the rule this way: a trust may be revoked by complying with any method the trust instrument provides; if the instrument explicitly makes that method exclusive, the trust may be revoked only in that manner; if not, the trust may also be revoked by a writing, signed by the settlor and delivered to the trustee; and unless the trust provides otherwise, a trust may be modified by these same revocation procedures.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Under current law, a trust may be revoked by complying with any method provided in the trust instrument. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(1).) If the trust explicitly makes that method exclusive, then it may be revoked only in that manner. If not, then the trust may also be revoked by a writing, other than a will, signed by the trustor and delivered to the trustee while the trustor is alive. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(2).) Unless the trust provides otherwise, the trust may be modified by the revocation procedures of Probate Code section 15401. (Prob. Code, § 15402.)"
  — Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956 (California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District), overview of the exclusive-method rule under Probate Code sections 15401-15402 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259556/huscher-v-wells-fargo-bank/)
  Known gap: This clause draws on the same Probate Code section 15401(a)(2) 'exclusive method' language already quoted in a separate clause of this document addressing the general revocation procedure, plus one independent source: a published California Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision. A search for a California Supreme Court decision squarely deciding whether a trust instrument's stated amendment method can be made exclusive did not turn up one on that specific question -- the most relevant California Supreme Court decision this search located, Donkin v. Donkin (2013) 58 Cal.4th 412, addresses a different question (how post-2010 no-contest-clause law applies to a trust amendment), not the exclusive-method question, so it is not cited here. The Court of Appeal decision quoted here, Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956, states the current-law rule in an overview passage, but the trust at issue in that case was created before July 1, 1987, so the court's actual holding turned on interpreting a prior Civil Code provision rather than on Probate Code sections 15401-15402 directly; the quoted passage is the court's own description of 'current law,' not the basis of its holding in that case. This is one state's case law and statute, used as real evidence -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust.

THE CAPACITY STANDARD FOR AMENDING A TRUST
The Probate Code sets a general legal-capacity standard that, by its own terms, applies to a person's capacity 'to execute trusts,' among other acts. That general standard applies 'except where otherwise provided by law' -- and the statute setting that general standard itself lists 'the statutory and decisional law of testamentary capacity' as an example of law that can displace it. A published California Court of Appeal decision has held that when a settlor's trust amendment, in its content and complexity, closely resembles a will or codicil, it is that lower, will-specific testamentary-capacity standard -- not the Probate Code's general capacity statute standing alone -- that a court should use to evaluate the settlor's capacity to make the amendment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except where otherwise provided by law, including, but not limited to, Section 813 and the statutory and decisional law of testamentary capacity, a person lacks the capacity to make a decision unless the person has the ability to communicate verbally, or by any other means, the decision, and to understand and appreciate, to the extent relevant, all of the following: (a) The rights, duties, and responsibilities created by, or affected by the decision. (b) The probable consequences for the decisionmaker and, where appropriate, the persons affected by the decision. (c) The significant risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives involved in the decision."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 812 (California Legislative Information text), the general capacity standard and its carve-out for testamentary-capacity law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=812.)
  "(a) A determination that a person is of unsound mind or lacks the capacity to make a decision or do a certain act, including, but not limited to, the incapacity to contract, to make a conveyance, to marry, to make medical decisions, to execute wills, or to execute trusts, shall be supported by evidence of a deficit in at least one of the following mental functions, subject to subdivision (b), and evidence of a correlation between the deficit or deficits and the decision or acts in question: ... (b) A deficit in the mental functions listed above may be considered only if the deficit, by itself or in combination with one or more other mental function deficits, significantly impairs the person's ability to understand and appreciate the consequences of his or her actions with regard to the type of act or decision in question."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 811(a), (b) (California Legislative Information text), the general-capacity evidentiary standard, expressly covering the act of executing a trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=811.)
  "When determining whether a trustor had capacity to execute a trust amendment that, in its content and complexity, closely resembles a will or codicil, we believe it is appropriate to look to section 6100.5 to determine when a person's mental deficits are sufficient to allow a court to conclude that the person lacks the ability 'to understand and appreciate the consequences of his or her actions with regard to the type of act or decision in question.' (§ 811, subd. (b).) In other words, while section 6100.5 is not directly applicable to determine competency to make or amend a trust, it is made applicable through section 811 to trusts or trust amendments that are analogous to wills or codicils."
  — Andersen v. Hunt (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 722 (California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District), holding that the testamentary-capacity standard applies to a trust amendment resembling a will or codicil, via section 811(b) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5810338/andersen-v-hunt/)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence of how California determines the capacity standard applicable to a trust amendment -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust amendment, or about the capacity of any specific person to amend a specific trust. The Court of Appeal decision quoted here, Andersen v. Hunt (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 722, held that the will-specific standard (Probate Code section 6100.5) applies to a trust amendment only because it is incorporated through Probate Code section 811, subdivision (b) -- the court expressly said that section 6100.5 'is not directly applicable to determine competency to make or amend a trust' on its own, and that whether the will-specific standard controls a given amendment can depend on how closely, 'in its content and complexity,' that amendment resembles a will or codicil. This document does not attempt to resolve that content-and-complexity question for any particular amendment. This is a Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision; this search did not identify a California Supreme Court decision resolving the same question.

A TRUST WITH MORE THAN ONE SETTLOR
If a trust has more than one settlor -- as is common for a married couple's joint trust -- the same statute that supplies the default modification procedure also addresses, separately from the single-settlor case, what each settlor may do on their own. Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, where a trust is created by more than one settlor, each settlor may revoke -- and, through the modification statute's cross-reference, modify -- the trust as to the portion of the trust that settlor contributed, subject to a Family Code provision governing community property. A settlor may also grant another person, including a spouse, a power to revoke or modify all or part of that settlor's own contributed portion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) (1) Unless otherwise provided in the instrument, if a trust is created by more than one settlor, each settlor may revoke the trust as to the portion of the trust contributed by that settlor, except as provided in Section 761 of the Family Code. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a settlor may grant to another person, including, but not limited to, his or her spouse, a power to revoke all or part of that portion of the trust contributed by that settlor, regardless of whether that portion was separate property or community property of that settlor, and regardless of whether that power to revoke is exercisable during the lifetime of that settlor or continues after the death of that settlor, or both."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(b) (California Legislative Information text), revocation and modification where a trust has more than one settlor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15401.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's revocation-and-modification statute addresses a trust with more than one settlor -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific joint trust, and not a claim about how any specific joint trust's own terms should be read. This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Probate Code section 15401, the same statutory section already quoted (subdivision (a)) in a separate clause of this document addressing the single-settlor default procedure; it is presented as its own clause because subdivision (b) addresses a distinct question. The statute's cross-reference to Family Code section 761, governing community property held in trust, is not independently quoted or researched here. Beyond this subdivision, no additional statute specific to joint or shared trusts addressing modification was located; whether unanimous consent, majority action, or some other rule applies to jointly contributed or community property held in a specific joint trust can depend on that trust's own terms and on the community-property characterization of the property involved, neither of which this document resolves.

'AMENDMENT' VERSUS 'RESTATEMENT' IS A DRAFTING CONVENTION, NOT A SEPARATE STATUTE
California's Probate Code does not use or define the term 'restatement' anywhere in its trust-modification provisions. Whether a settlor changes a trust by executing a document labeled an 'amendment' that alters specific provisions, or by executing a document labeled an 'amendment and restatement' that replaces the entire body of the trust instrument while keeping the same underlying trust in existence, both are exercises of the same statutory modification power: the settlor's ability, unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, to modify the trust by the procedure for revocation. The choice between amending discrete provisions and restating the whole instrument is a drafting convention, not a distinct legal mechanism with its own statutory requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, if a trust is revocable by the settlor, the settlor may modify the trust by the procedure for revocation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15402 (California Legislative Information text), the modification power, which does not distinguish 'amendment' from 'restatement' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15402.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's trust-modification statute does not distinguish between an 'amendment' and a 'restatement' as separate legal categories -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This clause quotes the same single-sentence statute, Probate Code section 15402, already quoted in full in a separate clause of this document addressing the general statutory basis for modification; it is repeated here only because this clause makes a distinct point about that statute's scope -- that it does not carve out 'restatement' as something different from 'modification' -- and no independent second source using 'restatement' as a term of art was located in the statute itself.

RATIFICATION OF ALL OTHER TRUST PROVISIONS
Except as specifically changed by this amendment, I confirm that all other provisions of the Trust remain unchanged and in full force and effect. This amendment does not revoke the Trust; the Trust, as amended by this instrument and by any prior amendments, continues without interruption.

SIGNATURE AND NOTARIZATION
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Jordan Alex Lee, as settlor, has signed this amendment to The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust on the date written below.

_________________________ Date: _________________________
Jordan Alex Lee, Settlor

Delivery of a signed writing to Jordan Alex Lee is one of the statutory methods described elsewhere in this document for satisfying the procedure that California's modification statute incorporates, unless The Jordan Alex Lee Revocable Living Trust's own instrument makes a different method exclusive.

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.
